title: Roth conversion: 3 numbers that decide
audience: People with traditional IRA money considering a partial Roth conversion
thesis: A Roth conversion is a one-way bet on your future tax rate. Three numbers decide: current bracket, expected future bracket, and the conversion size.

concepts.label: Current bracket
concepts.body: Your current marginal tax bracket is the cost of converting. Convert $50,000 from a 24% bracket — the IRS treats that $50,000 as ordinary income this year. You pay $12,000 in federal tax (24% × $50,000) on the conversion.

concepts.label: Future bracket expectation
concepts.body: The conversion pays off if your future marginal bracket is higher than today's. RMDs at 73, Social Security taxation, RSU vesting — all push future income up. The current TCJA brackets sunset after 2025; absent extension, the 24% bracket becomes 25% in 2026.
concepts.source: IRC §1 (bracket inflation adjustments); TCJA sunset provisions

concepts.label: Conversion size and the bracket-fill
concepts.body: Convert up to the top of your current bracket, not a penny more. Stay in the 24% bracket — convert $20,000 or $50,000, but don't cross into 32%. Bracket-fill maximizes the conversion while minimizing the marginal rate.
concepts.source: IRS Pub 590-A conversion strategy; IRC §1 tax brackets
